summary: This document deprecates the BGP Entropy Label Capability attribute defined in RFC 6790. That RFC required routers that cannot process Entropy Labels to remove the attribute, but this cannot be guaranteed in practice, so the attribute is unreliable.

plainLanguage.summary: The BGP Entropy Label Capability attribute could pass through routers that did not understand it, even though those routers were expected to remove it. RFC 7447 retires the attribute and says implementations must not create it.

questions: why was the bgp elca deprecated
what is the entropy label capability attribute
why was the bgp entropy label capability attribute deprecated
subtitle: Deprecates a BGP attribute whose removal requirement could not be met reliably.

tldr.problem: The BGP Entropy Label Capability attribute had to be removed by nodes unable to process entropy labels, but optional, transitive attributes are propagated by nodes that do not recognize them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC deprecates the attribute: implementations MUST NOT generate it and MUST treat a received instance as an unrecognized optional, transitive attribute.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7447 updates RFC 6790 and records BGP path attribute 28 as deprecated; a forthcoming document was to propose a replacement.

today: RFC 7447 is a Proposed Standard from February 2015 and updates RFC 6790 by deprecating the ELCA defined in its Section 5.2.

sections.title: Why the Attribute Was Deprecated
sections.content:
RFC 6790 defines the Entropy Label Capability attribute (ELCA) as an optional, transitive BGP path attribute. A node that changes a route's next hop must remove the attribute unless it can process entropy labels.

The RFC explains why this requirement cannot be guaranteed: a node that does not support an optional, transitive attribute propagates it. Such a node is likely unable to process entropy labels, so it may pass along the very attribute it was supposed to remove.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that did not understand this attribute could pass it onward. That conflicts with the rule that such routers should remove it, so the RFC retires the attribute.

sections.title: Required Handling
sections.content:
Implementations MUST NOT generate ELCA. If an implementation receives it, it MUST treat it like any other unrecognized optional, transitive attribute under RFC 4271, until a new specification reuses the code point.

The deprecation applies to the version defined in Section 5.2 of RFC 6790. Other sections of RFC 6790 are unchanged. The memo says that, to the authors' best knowledge, there were no implementations of ELCA at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not create ELCA. If it arrives, handle it as an unrecognized optional, transitive attribute unless a later specification reuses its code point.

sections.title: Registry and Security Effects
sections.content:
IANA marked attribute 28, the BGP Entropy Label Capability Attribute, as deprecated in the BGP Path Attributes registry. The memo says a receiver might improperly rely on a tunneled attribute, which could create a black hole in the forwarding path for affected routes.

The RFC notes that exploitation would require an attacker to be on the control-plane path. It says deprecating ELCA makes any real or imagined security issues with it moot.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA marked attribute 28 as deprecated. The RFC says relying on an attribute passed through routers could misdirect routes, and deprecation removes that issue.
